extracted.intended_audience: general readers, TV/comedy fans, and television producers/interested practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit production/evaluation criteria for an adult-oriented puppet television series built around real prank/crank calls and puppet re-enactments. Covers format, legal/production constraints, character development, and episode structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use actual crank calls with puppet re-enactments
rubrics_metrics.description: "It features actual crank calls made by show regulars and celebrity guests, with on-screen re-enactments by puppets."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core format requirement: episodes are built around recorded prank/crank calls which are then reenacted visually with puppets. The article frames this as the show's defining premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer improvisation from writer premises
rubrics_metrics.description: "The performers are given a basic outline of a premise by the writers, and call telephone numbers from a list of selected targets (known as 'marks'). Using the basic premises, the performers improvise most of their lines, playing off of the responses of their marks, with the intention to keep them on the phone as long as possible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production practice: writers supply basic premises and target numbers; performers must be skilled at improvisation and reactive comedy, aiming to sustain the call and generate material from the mark's replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record calls in a jurisdiction permitting one-party consent (Nevada)
rubrics_metrics.description: "With the exception of a few outside sources..., all the calls are made from Nevada. The Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 makes it illegal in eleven states to record telephone calls without both parties' consent. Under Nevada law, only one of the parties has to give consent (i.e., the caller), so prank calls can be recorded without the consent of the prank victims."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/ethical constraint: producers must ensure call recordings comply with state and federal wire/recording laws; the show records from Nevada to rely on one-party consent. Planning must account for differing state laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design puppets based on marks' voices and stock character voices
rubrics_metrics.description: "The puppet designs were drawn by artist Todd James before being constructed based on the various marks' voices, and, along with a series of stock characters... based on the performers' character voices, the calls are re-enacted for the skits."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative guideline: puppet appearance should be informed by the recorded voice/tone and the character being portrayed; establishing distinctive stock characters tied to performer voices supports recurring gags and audience familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build production capacity (specialized builders and in-house puppet shop)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The main character puppets for the first season were constructed by Bob Flanagan's company Den Design with additional puppets built by... An in-house puppet shop was set up for the following seasons to accommodate the fast-paced schedule of the show and the sheer volume of puppet characters required for each episode."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational requirement: ensure access to skilled puppet builders and/or an in-house shop to meet the demands of high character volume and a fast production pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/branding vetting to avoid titles implying malice
rubrics_metrics.description: "Originally, the show was titled Prank Puppets; it was renamed after Comedy Central lawyers deemed that it implied malice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title and branding should be reviewed for legal and reputational exposure; avoid names or branding that could be construed as encouraging wrongdoing or malice to reduce legal risk and network concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and use recurring stock characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists many recurring stock characters (e.g., Niles Standish, Special Ed, Dick Birchum, Jimmy, Bobby Fletcher) that are used across calls and episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative/design guideline: employ a roster of recognizable stock characters (with catchphrases, recurring behaviors) to create continuity, facilitate improvisation, and build audience attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ celebrity guest voices to augment episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The show features many notable performers and celebrity guests providing voices across episodes (long list of comedians, actors, and musicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programming/marketing strategy: guest stars broaden appeal, diversify material, and can help attract viewers; coordinate guest schedules and recording logistics accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode structure, length, and mixed content
rubrics_metrics.description: "Running time 21–22 minutes" and episodes contain multiple prank-call skits and sometimes musical performances or guest segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format guideline: plan episodes to fit into ~21–22 minute broadcast slots, sequencing several short prank-call sketches (and occasional musical or special segments) to maintain pacing and variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt format to contemporary platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: "The new season includes pranks on social media and other platforms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evolution guideline: update prank sources and distribution strategies (e.g., social media, digital platforms) to reflect changing media consumption and maximize reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retire or revise characters deemed offensive to modern audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: "Special Ed ... is not present in the 2019 revival due to the character being deemed too offensive for modern audiences."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content-sensitivity guideline: review legacy characters/content for offensiveness and be prepared to alter or remove elements that do not align with current social standards or network policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate logistics around recording location and participant availability
rubrics_metrics.description: "One result of this was that production was fairly sporadic due to most of the celebrities living in Los Angeles and having limited availability to go to Las Vegas to make calls. Carolla, for example, took his radio program to Las Vegas once or twice a year, and while there would record new calls for the program."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling/logistics requirement: centralizing recording in a particular jurisdiction (for legal reasons) requires planning for talent travel or remote arrangements; production cadence may be affected by guest availability and travel constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit use of outside material and credit sources
rubrics_metrics.description: "With the exception of a few outside sources (including previous material from Jim Florentine and the Touch-Tone Terrorists), all the calls are made from Nevada."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights/credit guideline: when incorporating existing outside material, document permissions/credits and limit reliance on third-party material; prefer original calls to avoid rights issues and maintain consistent production methods.
